title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
text:
Information sheet

An overview of the project
As a citizen scientist, you will be given approximately 1 kg of perennial bread rye flour. You will need to purchase any additional ingredients you need to do your baking. You will be asked to take notes during your baking and use them to fill out a follow-up survey. Upon completion of the follow-up survey, you will be sent a small thank you gift (see Figure 1).
In 2027, the project will also host a field day where you can see the perennial bread rye growing, and in the fall there will be a symposium to share current knowledge about perennial bread rye with everyone across the value chain (researchers, breeders, farmers, millers, bakers, and bread eaters). Attendance to those events is free, and optional.
This citizen science project is part of a NNF Plant2Food research project (Grant #NNF22SA0081019) being conducted at the Department of Agroecology and Food Science at Aarhus University in Denmark in collaboration with Meyers, as well as Wageningen University and Research in the Netherlands. It is important to us to engage our communities in research to share what we are learning and also learn from each of you.


More detailed background and resources for the curious
Broadly speaking, all plants fall roughly into two categories: perennial and annual. Perennial plants live for more than one year, while annual plants do not. In nature, perennial plants are very common. Think of a neighborhood park: there will be trees, grass, maybe some roses. These are all perennial plants. In contrast, if you think of your kitchen garden, many of those plants are annuals, and you have to re-plant them every year (for example radishes, lettuce, or cucumbers). This general pattern of ‘perennials in nature, annuals in agriculture’ is actually seen at a global scale. And while we do have a lot of wonderful perennial crops, the crops we use the most (and the ones we plant on the most land) are annuals.



Globally, perennial plants are much more common compared to annuals. There is an over-representation of annuals in our agricultural crops, which is even more pronounced when you look at the area planted to annual versus perennial crops. Crops we use to make breads (wheat, barley, rye, maize, oats, sorghum, teff, millet, rice) are all annual crops. Figure created by Virginia Nichols.


Did humans just happen to domesticate annual crops for their staple foods? Or are annual plants just superior to perennials for food production? These questions are currently being debated. However, regardless of how we got here, everyone seems to agree that having more perennials integrated into our agricultural land, in some way, would be good for the environment. This is because perennials tend to offer benefits to the overall environment; they help put carbon into the soil, they provide soil cover year-round, and they use resources like water and nitrogen more efficiently.
Society has long recognized the potential benefits of a perennial grain. There have been efforts to breed perennial wheat in the Soviet Union since the 1930s! In the past, it has been a very difficult task, mainly because scientists had few tools to see what was going on inside the plant’s genetics. Despite these challenges, a few laboratories got lucky and had some successes, including one in Germany at the University of Hohenheim. There, Dr. Reimann-Philips and his team successfully crossed an annual rye with a perennial ancestor in the 1960s. The team tested the results, and made more selections. The resulting crop was perennial (Figure 3), and in 199X it was submitted to be considered as a variety in Germany.



Annual bread rye is sown in the fall, and the crop dies in late summer before the grain is harvested. Perennial bread rye is also sown in the fall, and while the growth from that year dies and grain is harvested just like in the annual crop, the roots stay alive and the crop regrows once light can hit the base of the plant. This new growth acts just like a crop that is sown in the fall…except you didn’t have to sow it.


But…the government didn’t think anyone would want to grow such a crop, so it was pushed aside to study new and more promising things. The breeders maintained some plots as a passion project, but it hasn’t gotten anyone’s full attention for the past thirty years. In 2023, Dr. Thomas Miedaner, who took over the University of Hhenheim’s rye breeding program after Dr. Reimann-Philips’ passing, shared some seeds of this neglected and forgotten crop with researchers at Aarhus University.
In 2025 we tested it side-by-side against a high-yielding annual rye. We were very impressed when it produced half of the grain yield of the modern annual, given that it was crossed with varieties from the 1960s! We think this variety deserves more development, and this grant is part of that effort. One of the goals of the grant is to understand how this new perennial bread rye performs in home kitchens, and to hear how people feel about this new perennial grain.

title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
text:
Answers to some common questions

Is this perennial bread rye genetically modified using new breeding technologies?
No, this variety was developed using traditional breeding methods, involving crossing plants by hand, and making selections based on their physical characteristics.


Is it safe to eat?
Yes. The European Union recognizes it as a safe food to eat, due to its genetic background and similarity to annual cereal rye. The grain used to make the flour was also tested at an independent laboratory for commercial use, which included an analysis of mycotoxins. You can access the lab results [here — link to be added] and they will be sent to you along with the flour.


Is this grain organic?
Aarhus University does not have any organically certified land due to the costs and additional administrative complexity that would entail. However, this grain was grown without the use of pesticides.


Can I buy this flour somewhere?
Perennial bread rye is not currently available commercially, however it may be in the near future.


How long would this crop continue to produce grain?
It has not been tested extensively at this point, but it seems the perennial cereal rye reliably produces grain for at least two years. After this time weeds and diseases may become problems, but we need more research to determine the optimal way to manage the crop.

title: About this website
text:
About this website
This website was built to provide access to documents related to the GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation, a home baking initiative that is part of the larger GoodGrain research grant. On this website you can access:

Informational Sheet in English
Informational Sheet in Danish
Videos in English

The Informational Video
‘For the Curious’ Video

The lab results from the flour: GoodGrain Lab Results (PDF)

The big picture of this research is to explore how perennial cereal rye might contribute to more sustainable food systems. We are researching how the crop behaves in the field, however important questions remain about the safety, quality, and nutritional properties of grain harvested from perennial rye.
The GoodGrain project investigates these questions by:

Evaluating grain and baking quality, from laboratory analyses to bakery trials.
Exploring relationships between perennial cropping, soil health, and potentially beneficial nutritional compounds such as ergothioneine.
Assessing natural contaminants, including fungal alkaloids, in perennial and annual rye.
Connecting researchers with farmers, food businesses, retailers, and policymakers, and sharing results openly.

The Home Baking Project brings this research into people’s kitchens. By inviting participants to bake with rye flour and share their experiences, we aim to learn more about how perennial rye flour performs in everyday baking and how people respond to it.
Learn more about the wider research project on the GoodGrain project website.

title: GoodGrain – hjemmebagningsevaluering
text:
Informationsark

Oversigt over projektet
Som borgerforsker får du cirka 1 kg mel af flerårig rug til brødbagning. Du skal selv købe de øvrige ingredienser, du har brug for til bagningen. Vi beder dig om at tage noter undervejs i bagningen og bruge dem til at udfylde et opfølgende spørgeskema. Når du har udfyldt spørgeskemaet, får du en lille tak-for-hjælpen-gave (se figur 1).
I 2027 arrangerer projektet også en markdag, hvor du kan se den flerårige rug vokse. Om efteråret afholder vi et symposium, hvor vi deler den aktuelle viden om flerårig rug til brødbagning med alle led i værdikæden (forskere, forædlere, landmænd, møllere, bagere og brødspisere). Det er gratis og frivilligt at deltage i begge arrangementer.
Dette borgerforskningsprojekt er en del af et NNF Plant2Food-forskningsprojekt (bevilling nr. NNF22SA0081019), der gennemføres ved Institut for Agroøkologi og Institut for Fødevarer på Aarhus Universitet i Danmark i samarbejde med Meyers samt Wageningen University & Research i Nederlandene. Det er vigtigt for os at inddrage vores lokalsamfund i forskningen, så vi kan dele det, vi lærer, og samtidig lære af jer.


Mere baggrund og ressourcer for de nysgerrige
Overordnet kan planter inddeles i to kategorier: flerårige og etårige. Flerårige planter lever i mere end ét år, mens etårige planter ikke gør. Flerårige planter er meget almindelige i naturen. Tænk for eksempel på en park i dit nabolag: Der er måske træer, græs og nogle roser. Det er alt sammen flerårige planter. I køkkenhaven er mange planter derimod etårige, og dem skal man så eller plante igen hvert år – for eksempel radiser, salat og agurker. Dette generelle mønster med »flerårige planter i naturen, etårige planter i landbruget« ses faktisk på globalt plan. Selvom vi har mange gode flerårige afgrøder, er de afgrøder, vi bruger mest – og dyrker på det største areal – etårige.



På globalt plan er flerårige planter langt mere almindelige end etårige planter. Etårige planter er overrepræsenterede blandt vores landbrugsafgrøder, og forskellen er endnu tydeligere, når man ser på det areal, der dyrkes med henholdsvis etårige og flerårige afgrøder. De afgrøder, vi bruger til at fremstille brød (hvede, byg, rug, majs, havre, sorghum, teff, hirse og ris), er alle etårige. Figuren er udarbejdet af Virginia Nichols.


Var det blot et tilfælde, at mennesker domesticerede etårige afgrøder til deres basale fødevarer? Eller er etårige planter simpelthen bedre end flerårige til fødevareproduktion? Disse spørgsmål diskuteres stadig. Uanset hvordan vi er nået hertil, synes der dog at være bred enighed om, at det på en eller anden måde ville være godt for miljøet at integrere flere flerårige planter i vores landbrugsarealer. Flerårige planter har ofte miljømæssige fordele: De bidrager til at lagre kulstof i jorden, holder jorden dækket året rundt og udnytter ressourcer som vand og kvælstof mere effektivt.
Samfundet har længe anerkendt de mulige fordele ved flerårige kornafgrøder. Der har været forsøg på at forædle flerårig hvede i Sovjetunionen siden 1930’erne! Tidligere var det en meget vanskelig opgave, især fordi forskerne havde få redskaber til at undersøge, hvad der foregik i planternes genetik. Trods udfordringerne havde nogle få laboratorier held med arbejdet, blandt andet et ved Universität Hohenheim i Tyskland. Her krydsede Dr. Reimann-Philips og hans team i 1960’erne med succes en etårig rug med en flerårig slægtning. Teamet afprøvede afkommet og udvalgte yderligere planter. Resultatet var en flerårig afgrøde (figur 3), som i 199X blev indsendt til vurdering som sort i Tyskland.



Etårig rug til brødbagning sås om efteråret, og planten dør sidst på sommeren, inden kornet høstes. Flerårig rug til brødbagning sås også om efteråret. Væksten fra det pågældende år visner, og kornet høstes ligesom i den etårige afgrøde, men rødderne forbliver levende. Afgrøden vokser igen, når der kommer lys ned til plantens basis. Den nye vækst fungerer som en afgrøde, der er sået om efteråret – bortset fra, at man ikke behøvede at så den.


Men myndighederne mente ikke, at nogen ville være interesseret i at dyrke en sådan afgrøde, og arbejdet blev derfor lagt til side til fordel for undersøgelsen af nye og mere lovende muligheder. Forædlerne holdt nogle forsøgsparceller ved lige som et passioneret fritidsprojekt, men afgrøden har ikke fået fuld opmærksomhed i de seneste tredive år. I 2023 delte Dr. Thomas Miedaner, der overtog rugforædlingsprogrammet ved Universität Hhenheim efter Dr. Reimann-Philips’ død, frø fra denne oversete og glemte afgrøde med forskere ved Aarhus Universitet.
I 2025 afprøvede vi den side om side med en højtydende etårig rug. Vi var meget imponerede over, at den gav halvdelen af kornudbyttet fra den moderne etårige sort, når man tager i betragtning, at den blev krydset med sorter fra 1960’erne! Vi mener, at sorten fortjener videreudvikling, og denne bevilling er en del af indsatsen. Et af bevillingens mål er at undersøge, hvordan denne nye flerårige rug til brødbagning fungerer i hjemmekøkkener, og at høre, hvad folk synes om denne nye flerårige kornafgrøde.

title: GoodGrain – hjemmebagningsevaluering
section: Svar på nogle ofte stillede spørgsmål
text:
Svar på nogle ofte stillede spørgsmål

Er denne flerårige rug til brødbagning genetisk modificeret ved hjælp af nye forædlingsteknologier?
Nej. Sorten er udviklet ved hjælp af traditionelle forædlingsmetoder, hvor planter krydses manuelt, og udvælgelsen baseres på deres fysiske egenskaber.


Er den sikker at spise?
Ja. Den Europæiske Union anerkender den som en fødevare, der er sikker at spise, på grund af dens genetiske baggrund og lighed med etårig rug. Kornet, der blev brugt til at fremstille melet, er desuden blevet testet af et uafhængigt laboratorium med henblik på kommerciel anvendelse. Testen omfattede blandt andet en analyse for mykotoksiner. Du kan finde laboratorieresultaterne [her – link tilføjes]. De bliver også sendt til dig sammen med melet.


Er denne rug økologisk?
Aarhus Universitet har ikke økologisk certificerede arealer, fordi certificeringen medfører omkostninger og yderligere administrativt arbejde. Denne rug blev dog dyrket uden brug af pesticider.


Kan jeg købe dette mel et sted?
Flerårig rug til brødbagning er endnu ikke tilgængelig på markedet, men det kan muligvis ændre sig i den nærmeste fremtid.


Hvor længe vil afgrøden fortsætte med at producere korn?
Afgrøden er endnu ikke blevet undersøgt grundigt, men det ser ud til, at den flerårige rug pålideligt producerer korn i mindst to år. Derefter kan ukrudt og sygdomme blive et problem, men der er behov for mere forskning for at fastslå, hvordan afgrøden bedst dyrkes og plejes.

title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
text:
Introduction
If you are receiving this Informational Sheet, it means you have expressed interest in conducting a home baking evaluation using a new perennial variety of rye. Thank you! This sheet is meant to give you more information about this new variety, so you can decide if you would like to participate.



Reading this Informational Sheet is meant to aid you in your decision of whether or not to participate in the GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation. Attendance to the GoodGrain field day GoodGrain and symposium are optional, and are not required for participation in the Home Baking Evaluation.




What happens next?

Watch the [Informational Video — link to be added] (in English) and/or read this Informational Sheet in English or Danish.
After watching the video and/or reading, if you decide you would like to participate in our research, complete the [intake form — link to be added].



An overview of the project
All of the crops we commonly use to make bread (for example wheat, oats, rye, barley) are annuals, meaning they are sown and produce one grain harvest, then must be sown again. If a crop could produce two or three grain harvests from one sowing, it would save the farmer a lot of work (and tractor driving), and by allowing the crop to remain in the field and develop more roots, it may also create better environmental outcomes. Recently, a few varieties of perennial grains have been developed, including a perennial rye grain. This new variety is being tested in the field to evaluate how it grows in Denmark, as well as how it impacts the environment as compared to an annual rye crop. The GoodGrain project is meant to build on that knowledge by looking specifically at the new perennial rye’s grain characteristics. One of those characteristics is its baking quality. It is important to the GoodGrain project to engage with our communities in this effort. You can read a bit more about the GoodGrain project here.
As a citizen scientist supporting this effort, you will be given approximately 1 kg of rye flour from this new perennial variety. You will need to purchase any additional ingredients you need to do your baking. You will be asked to take notes during your baking and use them to fill out a follow-up survey. Upon completion of the follow-up survey, you will be sent a small thank you gift.
In the summer of 2027, the GoodGrain project will also host an event where you can see the perennial rye variety growing in the field in a test plot in Jutland. In the fall of 2027, there will be a public symposium in Copenhagen to share current knowledge about perennial rye with everyone across the value chain (researchers, breeders, farmers, millers, bakers, and bread eaters). The events are freely open to the public - we welcome you to attend, but it is optional.


Funding and project partners
This citizen science project is part of a NNF Plant2Food research project (Grant #NNF22SA0081019) being conducted at the Department of Agroecology and Department of Food Science at Aarhus University in Denmark in collaboration Wageningen University and Research in the Netherlands, and with Meyers, a prominent Danish food enterprise. As mentioned above, you can read a bit more about the GoodGrain project here.


Answers to some common questions

Is it safe to eat?
Yes. The grain used to make the flour you are receiving was tested at an independent laboratory to ensure it is safe for human consumption. You can access the lab results here: GoodGrain Lab Results (PDF).


Is this perennial rye variety genetically modified using new breeding technologies?
No, this variety was developed using traditional breeding methods, involving crossing plants by hand, and making selections based on their physical characteristics. You can read more about it in this scientific publication from 1986.


Is this grain organic?
No, Aarhus University does not have any organically certified land due to the costs and additional administrative complexity that would entail. However, this grain was grown without the use of pesticides.


Can I buy this flour somewhere?
Flour from this perennial rye variety is not currently available commercially. This project is laying the groundwork for a potential commercial release, and your help is appreciated!



For the curious
Broadly speaking, all plants fall roughly into two categories: perennial and annual. Perennial plants live for more than one year, while annual plants do not. In nature, perennial plants are very common. Think of a neighborhood park, or the forest: there will be trees, shrubs, maybe some grass. These are all perennial plants. In contrast, many of the plants in your kitchen garden are annuals, meaning you have to re-plant them every year (for example radishes, lettuce, or cucumbers). This general pattern of ‘perennials in nature, annuals in agriculture’ is actually seen at a global scale. And while we do have a lot of wonderful perennial crops (for example apples, avocados, and coffee!), the crops we use the most (and the ones we plant on the most land) are annuals, as you can see in the figure below.



In nature 94% of the plant species are perennial. Early human farmers seemed to prefer annuals, as 42% of the plants we have domesticated in some way are annuals. While less than half of the plants we have domesticated are annuals, most of our agricultural land is planted to annuals. This is because most of human calories come from annual crops, such as maize, rice, potatoes, and wheat. Crops we commonly use to make breads in Denmark (wheat, barley, rye, oats) are all annual crops. Figure created by Virginia Nichols.


Are annual plants just superior to perennials for food production? Did humans deliberately choose to domesticate annual crops? Or was it just coincidence? These questions are currently being debated. However, regardless of how we got here, it is clear that having more perennials integrated into our agricultural land would be good for the environment. This is because perennials tend to offer benefits to the overall environment; they help put carbon into the soil, they provide soil cover year-round, and they use resources like water and nitrogen more efficiently. Creating perennial versions of our staple crops, like the perennial rye used in this project, is one way to get more perennials onto our agricultural land.
Societies have long recognized the potential benefits of a perennial grain. There have been efforts to breed perennial wheat in the Soviet Union since the 1930s! In the past, it has been a very difficult task, mainly because scientists had few tools to see what was going on inside the plant’s genetics. Despite these challenges, a few laboratories got lucky and had some successes, including one in Germany at the University of Hohenheim. There, in the 1960s, Dr. Reimann-Philips and his team successfully crossed an annual rye with a old perennial rye ancestor. The team tested the results, and made more selections. The resulting crop was perennial (see figure below), and in the 1990s it was submitted to be considered as a variety in Germany.



Annual rye is sown in the fall, and the crop dies in late summer before the grain is harvested. Perennial rye is also sown in the fall, and while the growth from that year dies and grain is harvested just like in the annual crop, the roots stay alive and the crop regrows after harvest. This new growth acts just like a crop that is sown in the fall…except you didn’t have to sow it.


The German government rejected the application, and it was never released as a variety. The breeders maintained some plots as their passion project, and while some of the material was later released as a wildlife forage crop, the perennial rye hasn’t gotten anyone’s full attention for the past thirty years. In 2023, Dr. Thomas Miedaner, who took over the University of Hohenheim’s rye breeding program after Dr. Reimann-Philips’ passing, shared some seeds of this crop with researchers at Aarhus University, who think the idea of a perennial rye has a lot of potential in Denmark!
In 2025 we tested the perennial rye side-by-side against a high-yielding annual rye. We were very impressed when it produced half of the grain yield of the modern annual rye, given that it was crossed with varieties from the 1960s! The perennial rye produced grain again in 2026, but we need more research to determine the optimal way to manage the crop. We think this variety deserves more development, and this grant is part of that effort. One of the goals of the grant is to understand how this new perennial rye performs in home kitchens, and to understand how people feel about eating a perennial grain.

Mel fra denne flerårige rugsort er endnu ikke tilgængeligt i handelen. Projektet er med til at skabe grundlaget for en mulig fremtidig kommerciel lancering, og vi sætter stor pris på din hjælp!

title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
section: Make two versions of a baked good (1 or more days)
text:
Make two versions of a baked good (1 or more days)
As a citizen scientist home baker, we will provide you with either 400 or 800 grams of flour (based on your use needs). Our hope is that you will do a side-by-side baking experiment, using the perennial rye flour we provide and the rye flour you normally use.
You are welcome to mix the rye flour with other grains or flours if that is what you normally do. If you use a rye sourdough starter, you can try to use this rye in it. If you normally make crackers, or pizza dough, or cookies, that is fine too! We want to you to feel free to use the flour to make whatever brings you joy! But we ask that you try to be as scientific as you can, and bake your creation with both the perennial rye, and your normal rye.



Our hope is that you will do a side-by-side bake, using the perennial rye we provide and the rye you normally use. Image made with the help of AI.


Note that you will need to purchase any additional ingredients you need to do your baking.

title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
text:
Take notes
You will be provided with a sheet to guide your note-taking during your baking, which you can use to fill out the post-baking survey.

title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
text:
Fill out post-baking survey (15-30 minutes)
In the post-baking survey, there are three general sections:

Simple demographic information about everyone who was involved in the baking (we know some people may bake on their own, while others may bake with their kids, parents, or partners)
Questions about any differences you noticed between the product made with the perennial rye and the one made with the annual rye
Questions about your experience

We estimate the post-baking survey will require between 15-30 minutes to fill out. Depending on what you chose to bake, this project could take a full day to complete!

title: GoodGrain Home Baking Evaluation
section: Receive a small thank you gift
text:
Receive a small thank you gift
We understand this is a big time commitment, and upon completion of the post-baking survey, you will be sent a small thank you gift 🎁.

title: GoodGrain Hjemmebagningsevaluering
section: Lav to versioner af et bagværk (over 1 eller flere dage)
text:
Lav to versioner af et bagværk (over 1 eller flere dage)
Som borgerforsker vil du modtage enten 400 eller 800 gram mel, afhængigt af dit behov. Vi håber, at du vil gennemføre et bageforsøg, hvor du afprøver to versioner side om side: én med den flerårige rug, vi leverer, og én med den rug du normalt bruger.
Du er velkommen til at blande rugmelet med andre kornsorter eller meltyper, hvis det er sådan, du normalt gør. Hvis du bruger en rugsurdej kan du prøve at anvende den nye rug i den. Hvis du normalt bager knækbrød, laver pizzadej eller bager småkager er det også helt fint!
Vi vil gerne give dig frihed til at bruge melet til at bage lige det du har lyst til og som gør dig glad. Vi beder dig dog om at tilgå forsøget så systematisk som muligt og bage det du vælger, både med den flerårige rug og med den rug du normalt bruger.



Vi håber at du vil bage to versioner side om sideÆ en med den flerårige rug vi leverer og en med den rug du nomalt bruger. Billedet er lavet med hjælp fra AI.


Du skal selv købe eventuelle ekstra ingredienser, som du har brug for til bagningen.

title: GoodGrain Hjemmebagningsevaluering
text:
Tag noter
Du får udleveret et ark, der hjælper dig med at tage noter under bagningen. Du kan bruge noterne til at udfylde spørgeskemaet efter bagningen.

title: GoodGrain Hjemmebagningsevaluering
text:
Udfyld spørgeskemaet efter bagningen (15–30 minutter)
Spørgeskemaet efter bagningen består af tre overordnede dele:

Enkle demografiske oplysninger om alle, der deltog i bagningen (vi ved, at nogle bager alene, mens andre bager sammen med deres børn, forældre eller partner).
Spørgsmål om eventuelle forskelle, du bemærkede mellem det bagværk, der blev lavet med flerårigt rugmel, og det, der blev lavet med etårigt rugmel.
Spørgsmål om din oplevelse af bageprocessen.

Vi anslår, at det tager 15–30 minutter at udfylde spørgeskemaet efter bagningen. Afhængigt af, hvad du vælger at bage, kan det tage en hel dag at gennemføre projektet!

title: GoodGrain Hjemmebagningsevaluering
text:
Modtag en lille tak-for-hjælpen-gave
Vi er klar over, at det kræver en del tid, og når du har udfyldt det opfølgende spørgeskema, vil du modtage en lille tak-for-hjælpen-gave 🎁.
